stories.title: Webb shows how supernova dust chronicles star evolution
stories.summary: Mid-infrared observations of the supernova remnant Cassiopeia A by the James Webb Space Telescope have mapped the chemical makeup of individual dust clumps. The pattern of silica, carbon and other dust suggests that fusion shells inside the original star, such as its oxygen- and carbon-burning layers, mixed together possibly just hours before its core collapsed. The work gives astronomers a new way to reconstruct the layered structure of massive stars and the heavy elements they return to the galaxy.

stories.title: The secret of 'strange metals' may lie in quantum statistics, not collisions
stories.summary: In 'strange metals' such as the cuprate superconductors, electrical resistance grows linearly with temperature over a wide range, unlike in ordinary metals where electrons scatter off defects and lattice vibrations. Electrons in these materials appear to lose momentum as quickly as quantum mechanics permits, a limit named after Planck. The report suggests the explanation may come from quantum statistics rather than from collisions, although the cause remains unresolved.

stories.title: Photon fluctuations offer new way to probe electron dynamics in crystals
stories.summary: When strong laser pulses hit a crystal, it can give off light at frequencies many times that of the incoming beam, an effect called high-harmonic generation that lets scientists follow very fast electron motion. Instead of looking only at the brightness and spectrum of this light, researchers are now studying how the emission varies from one pulse to the next, which carries extra clues about how electrons in the solid produce the light.

stories.title: Unstable plasma heats itself with waves it generates, experiments reveal
stories.summary: Experiments suggest that an unstable plasma can produce its own waves, which then deposit energy back into the plasma and raise its temperature. This matters for fusion research, where very hot plasma is held in place by magnetic fields and is normally heated by injecting energetic particles or waves from outside. Self-heating of this kind could change how scientists think about reaching the high temperatures fusion needs.
